message.reasoning:
I need to decide on an auction bid for North Carolina Avenue.

I have $726 and a pink monopoly with four houses on each property. The opponent has only $29 and is building a dark blue monopoly. Player three is bankrupt.

Player four has a light blue monopoly and is the only remaining active bidder. The current bid for North Carolina Avenue is $105, so the next minimum bid is $106. I had previously capped my bids around $150 based on the property's mortgage value.

If I buy North Carolina Avenue for $150 or less and mortgage it, I recover the full amount. This denies player four a second green property, since they already own Pennsylvania Avenue.

Player four could trade with player one to complete a green monopoly, which would be devastating. Keeping the greens split prevents that. I will raise the bid to $106, staying under my $150 cap.

Unmortgaging the property later would cost $165. I am weighing whether the strategic value of blocking player four justifies paying slightly above the $150 mortgage value. Player four currently holds a dangerous light blue monopoly, two railroads, and mortgaged utilities.

Player four also owns a split orange set. Player one controls the dark blue monopoly with three houses on Park Place and four on Boardwalk. Boardwalk rent is $1,300 with four houses. That extreme threat makes blocking player four's green set even more critical.

I will not jump to $150. Player four has matched every bid so far, so they are committed and may push past that cap. A minimum raise keeps the auction open and forces them to pay more.

Player one has seven houses on dark blue and one on Marvin Gardens. Player four has twelve houses on light blue. The bank holds no houses, so no new construction is possible until properties are sold back.

Undeveloped green properties are not a major threat yet. The real danger is future building once houses are freed up through forced sales to pay rent. My $726 cash buffer is important because I could land on Boardwalk or Park Place.

I calculated the emergency cash needed if I land on Boardwalk. Selling all twelve pink houses returns about six hundred dollars. Mortgaging those properties adds roughly two hundred twenty more. Total emergency funds would reach about fifteen hundred forty-six dollars, still short of the one thousand seven hundred required.

Boardwalk with four houses is a bankruptcy risk even with full liquidation. Spending cash on North Carolina Avenue would shrink my survival buffer against the dark blue monopoly.

Bidding up to $150 and mortgaging immediately gives me $44 net cash. That improves my emergency reserves while blocking player four. At exactly $150, I pay $150 and mortgage back for $150, leaving my cash at $726.

Bidding $106 nets $44 cash after mortgaging. I should keep raising to $150. Each dollar above that costs me $50 net because the mortgage only returns $150. Denying player four is worth that sacrifice. If I drop at $150, they would pay $151 and still hold a dangerous property.

Player four could trade with player one to complete a green monopoly and acquire Pacific Avenue. Player one is cash-poor and might sell it. Player four already owns fully built light blue properties, but I am past them at Pennsylvania Avenue and will not land there again until I loop around. The immediate danger is player one's dark blue death zone ahead: Short Line, Chance, Park Place, Luxury Tax, and Boardwalk. Cash preservation for the next few rolls is critical.
